name: Negative calorie diet

lead: The negative calorie diet is built on the idea that some foods, mostly watery, fibrous, low-fat fruits and vegetables like celery, lettuce, grapefruit and cabbage, take more energy to digest than they contain. People use it to lose fat and look leaner.

The thermic effect of food is real, but measured values are a fraction of a food's calories; Wikipedia gives celery at about 8 percent. Weight loss on such diets is generally attributed to filling up on low-energy-density foods. A 2014 study found negative-calorie diets with exercise produced weight loss similar to low-calorie diets.

paras: In practice people build meals around foods on 'negative calorie' lists, such as celery, cucumber, lettuce, broccoli, cabbage, apples and citrus, often alongside plenty of water and exercise. Results come from the overall calorie deficit over weeks.
The main concern is nutritional adequacy if the diet is restricted to low-calorie produce; the chilled-water version would require very large volumes.

lead: The negative calorie diet is a dieting concept claiming that certain foods require more energy to digest and absorb than they provide. The foods listed are mostly low-calorie fruits and vegetables with high water and fibre content, such as celery, grapefruit, lemon, apple, lettuce, broccoli and cabbage.[1][2]
People adopt it to lose body fat and look leaner, often combined with exercise. The theory rests on the thermic effect of food, the energy spent digesting a meal.[2]

Researchers who have examined the idea report that the thermic effect of these foods is far smaller than their energy content, so none are calorically negative, while noting that diets rich in such foods can still produce weight loss.[3][2]

paras: The concept holds that the digestion cost of some foods exceeds their calories. Wikipedia notes the thermic effect of celery is roughly 8 percent, far below the 100 percent needed, and that chewing gum burns only about 11 kcal per hour.[2]

A bioRxiv examination of negative-calorie foods set out to test the idea empirically, noting that the existence of such foods has largely been argued against without a full empirical study.[3] Wikipedia reports that a 2005 plant-based diet study showed an average 13 lb loss over 14 weeks, credited to low energy density, fibre and thermic effect rather than negative calories.[2]
Diets limited to low-energy produce can fall short on protein and energy; the iced-water version would require dangerously large volumes, per Wikipedia.[2]

A 2014 Turkish Journal of Medical Sciences study compared a negative-calorie diet with a low-calorie diet, both with exercise, in overweight or obese men aged 45 to 75, examining weight loss and lipid profile; Wikipedia summarises that weight loss was similar between them.[1][2]
